recovered_records.title: Integrating deep learning into distributed hydrological modeling with physical constraints: unified streamflow prediction and reanalysis-supervised soil moisture representation over South Korea
recovered_records.abstract: Deep learning models have improved hydrological prediction, but their application to distributed modeling remains limited by weak physical consistency and the frequent separation of runoff generation from river routing. Here, we develop a physically constrained distributed Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework that jointly simulates reanalysis-supervised grid-scale soil moisture, runoff generation, and downstream streamflow through an end-to-end D8-based routing scheme. The framework incorporates soft constraints representing water balance, precipitation-based water availability, potential evapotranspiration limits, and soil moisture bounds. We evaluated the framework across South Korea using daily meteorological forcing, streamflow observations from 21 gauging stations, and a reanalysis-based soil moisture for 964 grid cells during 2005–2024. Temporal, spatial, and spatiotemporal validation experiments were conducted to assess predictive performance and transferability. The physically constrained model retained comparable performance at temporally held-out observations while providing its clearest benefits in ungauged basins. It achieved the highest median streamflow Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) under both the spatial validation (0.690 and 0.721) and spatiotemporal validation (0.688 and 0.640). These values exceeded those of the corresponding unconstrained distributed model by 0.049–0.080 for NSE and 0.089–0.162 for KGE. The learned internal responses satisfied the imposed bounds and exhibited hydrologically coherent changes in timing, persistence, and sensitivity to antecedent wetness, although they should not be interpreted as independently validated physical fluxes. The results indicate that soft hydrological constraints can improve streamflow transferability across ungauged basins, even when they do not uniformly improve all prediction targets or evaluation settings.

recovered_records.title: Relating precipitation extremes to streamflow peaks using percentile-based correspondence and interpretable machine learning
recovered_records.abstract: The extent to which precipitation extremes translate into streamflow peaks is a critical part of the rainfall-runoff relationship. This paper focuses on the extent to which the upper 90th percentile precipitation extremes correspond to streamflow peaks above different percentiles. Specifically, precipitation extremes are paired with streamflow peaks by searching for event-specific discharge maxima and estimating empirical percentiles; the percentile-based correspondence is calculated as the hit rate to quantify the proportion of paired streamflow peaks above different percentile levels; furthermore, random forest models coupled with analyses based on SHapley Additive exPlanations are used to diagnose the effects of catchment attributes on the correspondence by accounting for feature importance and interaction effects. A case study is devised for the dataset of Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies across the continental United States. The results show that the median proportions of paired streamflow peaks exceeding the 80th, 90th and 95th percentiles are about 70%, 57% and 45%, respectively. For the upper 90th percentile streamflow peaks, the random forest model identifies the snow fraction as the dominant attribute, with its negative impacts shaped by its interaction with mean elevation. Among catchments with the highest 20% of snow fraction, the median hit rates remain 0.53 below 500 m and 0.57 between 500 and 1000 m, but drop to 0.14 above 1000 m. After constraining the snow fraction-elevation interactions, the five leading catchment attributes shift to mean high-flow duration, longitude, mean precipitation, streamflow elasticity and silt fraction. Overall, the results inform the interpretation of catchment-specific precipitation extremes for streamflow forecasting and flood warning.

recovered_records.title: A knowledge-guided machine learning framework for reconstructing climate-driven subsurface water dynamics from time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography
recovered_records.abstract: Understanding and anticipating climate-driven subsurface water dynamics is essential for assessing water availability and ecosystem function, yet it remains challenging in heterogeneous mountain environments. Time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (TL-ERT) provides spatially distributed observations of subsurface change but has been used mainly to monitor subsurface change rather than to model its evolution. Here, we develop a knowledge-guided machine learning framework to reconstruct the spatiotemporal evolution of subsurface resistivity from daily meteorological forcing and continuous TL-ERT observations on a monitored hillslope. Before training, the TL-ERT data were corrected to a common reference temperature to remove the direct temperature dependence of resistivity, allowing temporal resistivity changes to be interpreted as a proxy for subsurface water-content change. Three neural architectures were evaluated within a shared recursive framework using structured loss terms that preserve reconstruction accuracy, local spatial structure, and coherent temporal variation. All models reproduced the dominant seasonal patterns, and the PredRNN-based architecture performed best, with an RMSE of 9.5 Ω·m over held-out test windows. Under rolling recursive reconstruction without subsequent ground-truth resistivity observations, the framework maintained seasonally coherent trajectories within the observed record. Under a + 4 °C warming scenario, the simulated temperature-corrected resistivity showed earlier shallow spring decreases about 12% and slight shallow summer increases, with weaker responses at depth. Through a water-content conversion, these changes are consistent with earlier spring wetting and shallow summer drying. These results provide a site-specific proof of concept that continuous TL-ERT observations combined with knowledge-guided machine learning can reconstruct the seasonal evolution of subsurface resistivity within the observed record and support scenario-based hydrologic interpretation.

recovered_records.title: Unearthing dominant controls of precipitation – streamflow interaction using information theory and explainable AI in large-sample hydrology
recovered_records.abstract: Understanding the interaction between precipitation (P) and streamflow (Q) across different hydrological regions is essential for the comprehensive interpretation of the catchment’s behaviour. The present study quantifies the strength of the P–Q interaction using the information-theoretic metric Transfer Entropy (TE) across the Conterminous United States. Daily precipitation, streamflow and 38 other variables related to hydrologic, climatic, soil and vegetation characteristics for 554 catchments were analysed. To identify the dominant factors influencing the TE values at the continental and regional scales, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were employed. The Conterminous US is delineated into homogeneous regions using the Gaussian Mixture Model clustering technique, using TE values and the continental-scale dominant factors as input attributes. The dominant factors governing the P-Q interaction at each cluster are also determined. The results exhibit that the spatial variability in TE is delineated into eight distinct regimes, with the lowest and Highest P-Q interactions observed in mountainous snow-dominated regions and humid catchments, respectively, indicating the dominance of storage components and rainfall, respectively. The SHAP analysis further reveals that the combination of variables regulates P-Q interactions across clusters, with runoff timing, flow signatures, vegetation dynamics, and snow fraction emerging as important controls in different regions. Overall, the findings demonstrate that P-Q interactions vary systematically across hydroclimatic settings and are governed by region-specific combinations of climatic, hydrologic, and physiographic factors.

recovered_records.title: A physics-informed, soft-causal ensemble deep neural network for robust probabilistic water quality assessment in arid regions
recovered_records.abstract: Because reservoirs are critical assets for water supply in arid and semi-arid environments, safeguarding these resources is essential. Water quality assessment in such systems therefore requires predictive models that are not only accurate but also interpretable and capable of quantifying uncertainty. In this study, a Physics-Based Soft-Causal Ensemble Probabilistic Deep Neural Network (PBSCEP-DNN) was developed to predict the Water Quality Index (WQI), using 16,096 field measurements from an AAQ-RINKO Conductivity-Temperature-Depth (CTD) profiler. The model was constructed using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), ensuring that the network topology reflects hypothesized environmental dependency pathways, both direct predictive relationships and confounder-related influences, rather than an unrestricted, fully connected structure. The proposed framework’s novelty lies in combining a network architecture based on hypothesized environmental dependencies, regularized through an L2 penalty on direct-path weights, with a deep ensemble of five probabilistic neural networks to capture both point predictions and associated uncertainty in reservoir water quality dynamics. The proposed framework achieved RMSE = 1.324 ± 0.222, MAE = 0.452 ± 0.110, R2 = 0.795 ± 0.075, and empirical coverage of Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP) = 0.996 ± 0.003 for nominal 95% prediction intervals, indicating conservative overcoverage. Rather than optimizing point-prediction accuracy alone, the PBSCEP-DNN offers a more physically grounded and uncertainty-aware alternative to purely data-driven prediction.

recovered_records.title: A two-stage framework integrating information entropy and machine learning for rapid pollution source identification in looped river networks
recovered_records.abstract: Rapid source identification of sudden water pollution incidents in looped river networks remains challenging because of the complex connectivity, multiple transport pathways, and mixing at junctions. Pollution source identification has been widely studied in both surface water and groundwater systems, but studies focusing specifically on looped river networks remain limited. To address this gap, this study develops a two-stage framework integrating information entropy (IE) and machine learning (ML). Concentration and discharge time series measured at monitoring stations are first transformed into IE values, making the data more compact and easier to process. In the first stage, the IE values are used as inputs to ML models to identify the river containing the pollution source. In the second stage, the IE values are used to establish an IE-based empirical formula (IE-EF) that links IE to the exact source location in the identified river. The case study shows that the accuracy of river identification (RI) exceeds 98% in the first stage. In the second stage, the location identification (LI) error is generally less than 1 km. The proposed framework also demonstrates good stability and can support emergency water-quality management in looped river networks.

recovered_records.title: StreamFormer: A multi-resolution transformer for scalable global river streamflow prediction
recovered_records.abstract: Data-driven streamflow models based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have achieved strong predictive skill but rely on long daily meteorological input sequences that impose substantial data storage and computational costs when scaled globally. We introduce StreamFormer (SF), a Transformer-based architecture that combines a hydrologically informed Multi-Resolution Scheme (MRS) and Dual-Scale Patching (DSP) to preserve short-term meteorological signals at high resolution while progressively compressing long-term history at coarser scales, substantially reducing both input storage and computational cost. Using data from over 6200 gauge stations worldwide, SF achieves an NSE of 0.753 and KGE of 0.757 under the multi-resolution scheme, comparable to the standard 365-day baseline but at substantially lower computational cost. Critically, SF maintains or improves performance with the shortened multi-resolution scheme while LSTM performance degrades, suggesting that attention-based models are better suited to heterogeneous temporal inputs. Stratified analysis reveals that catchments with high snow fraction and aridity benefit most from long-term context. SF also achieves faster training and inference, lower GPU memory, and reduced input storage compared to both the standard LSTM and vanilla Transformer baseline. The study demonstrates that hydrological domain knowledge can be used to compress inputs while preserving predictive accuracy at much lower computational cost, supporting scalable operational global hydrological modeling.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed hydrological graph neural network for distributed daily streamflow prediction in directed river networks
recovered_records.abstract: The basin in high-altitude mountainous areas is constrained by sparse station networks, complex river networks, and significant non-stationary hydrological processes, making it difficult for traditional time series models to simultaneously consider spatial connectivity and physical consistency. To address this issue, we propose Physics-Informed Hydrological Graph Neural Network (PI-HydroGNN) for distributed daily streamflow prediction in directed river networks. It combines temporal feature extraction, upstream connectivity and topological inflow aggregation, graph-based topology message passing, and physical constraints in a unified framework to represent temporal dynamics, river-network connectivity, and local mass conservation. The model was evaluated through comparisons with independent station-wise LSTM, regional multi-output LSTM, GCN and SWAT, together with ablation experiments, multi-step forecasting, analysis of Quality Balance Violations and ungauged basin extrapolation. The results showed that PI-HydroGNN outperformed the benchmark models in the training, validation, and testing periods, with an average NSE of 0.84 during the testing period and a RMSE reduction of about 16% compared to station-wise LSTM. The ablation experiment results showed that all the modules we considered made significant contributions to the predictive performance and exhibited significant spatial heterogeneity. At Yangbajing, the model still maintains good simulation ability, with an NSE of 0.79 and an R2 of 0.80, providing preliminary evidence of its spatial extrapolation capability. Overall, this study demonstrates that combining prior knowledge of hydrological physics with graph learning offers a promising approach for streamflow prediction in complex river networks, and suggests potential for application in ungauged basins that should be further validated under broader hydro-climatic conditions.

recovered_records.title: A grid-informed physics-guided graph deep learning framework for interpretable distributed daily streamflow prediction
recovered_records.abstract: Watershed refined management requires accurate, spatially explicit, and physically interpretable frameworks for distributed daily streamflow prediction. However, process-based models (PBMs) may be constrained by structural assumptions and parameterized process representations, whereas data-driven models (DDMs) often lack physical consistency and hydrologically interpretable spatial dependencies. We developed a Grid-informed Physics-Guided Graph Deep Learning (GPGDL) framework that integrates GSWAT-derived hydrological representations with a GraphSAGE-BiLSTM model. GSWAT, a grid-based implementation of the Soil and Water Assessment Tool (SWAT), provides grid-resolved upstream–downstream routing for constructing a weighted directed hydrological graph, together with process information for the gauging-station nodes. The framework was evaluated for multi-site daily streamflow prediction at 15 gauging stations in the Xiangjiang River Basin. The residual-learning configuration implemented within GPGDL achieved the best overall testing performance among the evaluated benchmark and ablation models. Its testing-period mean Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) and coefficient of determination (R2) values were 0.754 and 0.771, respectively. Additional diagnostic experiments comparing GSWAT- and SWAT-based guidance showed that framework performance was jointly influenced by the quality of simulated intermediate hydrological information and the corresponding spatial graph representation. Graph-based interpretation (node, edge, and feature levels) indicated that streamflow prediction relied on a compact and hydrologically meaningful subgraph concentrated in the mid- to upper-basin region, and that the learned spatial dependencies were consistent with the basin’s confluence structure and runoff-routing processes. Overall, the proposed GPGDL framework demonstrates that grid-informed PBM-derived topological priors and hydrological process variables can serve as structured knowledge for graph deep learning, providing a promising pathway for coupling PBMs with DDMs and advancing physics-guided deep learning for interpretable watershed prediction.

recovered_records.title: Joint prediction of river discharge and suspended sediment load through a physics-informed capacity-supply decomposition framework
recovered_records.abstract: River discharge (RD) and suspended sediment load (SSL) are inherently coupled in river systems, yet existing data-driven models often fail to explicitly represent their physical linkage, which limits physical interpretability and may reduce robustness under extreme conditions. To address this issue, this study proposes a physics-informed capacity-supply decomposition (PCSD) framework for joint prediction of RD and SSL. The key idea is to reformulate SSL prediction as a sequential decomposition problem, in which sediment load is expressed as the product of a discharge-dependent transport-capacity term and a supply-related modulation term. In this way, RD prediction and SSL prediction are linked within a physically meaningful sequential structure. To further enhance physical consistency, several constraints were incorporated into the framework, including monotonic constraints in the RD branch, as well as discharge-sediment envelope, low-flow threshold, and proxy-supervision constraints in the sediment branch. The framework was evaluated in the Beijiang River Basin, China, using daily hydro-meteorological data from 1991 to 2010, and was compared against several benchmark data-driven models. Results showed that the proposed framework maintained high RD prediction accuracy while achieving the best point-estimate performance for SSL among the evaluated models. For one-step SSL prediction, PCSD achieved the best overall performance, with RMSE, NSE, R2, and KGE of 195 kg/s, 0.89, 0.90, and 0.94, respectively. Its advantage was especially evident under extreme flood conditions, where it reproduced major sediment peaks more accurately than all benchmark models. Additional multi-lead-time experiments showed that PCSD retained SSL prediction skill across 1–7-day forecasting horizons and consistently outperformed decomposition-based and conventional data-driven benchmarks. These results suggest that the proposed decomposition framework provides a physically interpretable approach with strong predictive performance for coupled hydro-sediment prediction.

recovered_records.title: A dual post-processing framework for probabilistic streamflow forecasting using deep learning ensembles: Integrating residual correction and Vine Copula-based BMA
recovered_records.abstract: Quantifying forecasting uncertainty and providing probabilistic streamflow forecasts are fundamental for flood and drought mitigation, reservoir operation, and water resources management. However, existing post-processing approaches usually address either residual error modeling or multi-model ensemble fusion, while few studies integrate them both. This study proposes a dual post-processing framework termed RC-VCBMA for multi-step probabilistic streamflow forecasting. To account for input, structural, and parameter‑related sources of ensemble diversity, ensemble forecast members are generated using GEFS forecast precipitation, three deep learning architectures, and multiple objective functions. A Mixture Density Network utilizing Countable Mixtures of Asymmetric Laplacians with LSTM backbone is then developed to generate time-varying mixture distributions of member-level hydrological residuals, enabling deterministic residual correction via the conditional expectation while capturing non-Gaussianity, autocorrelation, and heteroscedasticity. Building on the corrected members, a Vine Copula-based Bayesian Model Averaging method is further introduced to derive member-wise conditional posterior distributions by characterizing the three-dimensional dependence among baseline, observed, and forecast flows, and fuse them into an ensemble posterior distribution. The proposed framework is evaluated for 6-hourly multi-step inflow forecasting from 6 h to 48 h ahead for the Three Gorges Reservoir. Results show that compared with RC-HUPBMA, RC-VCBMA reduces WIS and CRPS by 15.3% and 13.5%, respectively. Compared with CMAL-DBMA, RC-VCBMA improves WIS and α_index by 8.1% and 6.8%, respectively, and reduces IGN by 3.713 on average, while remaining competitive in CRPS. Overall, RC-VCBMA achieves a favorable trade-off among distributional accuracy, interval sharpness, reliability, and predictive density concentration, highlighting its effectiveness as a probabilistic post-processing framework.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed neural networks for hydrodynamic inversion and discharge estimation in river flows over complex bed topography
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate estimation of river discharge and internal hydraulic states remains a fundamental challenge in hydrological monitoring, particularly when observations are limited and key flow variables cannot be directly measured. In this study, we develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN)-based framework for hydrodynamic inversion and discharge estimation in river flows over complex bed topography under limited observations. The proposed approach embeds the Serre–Green–Naghdi (SGN) equations into the neural network training process to enforce physical consistency while assimilating limited observations, such as water-depth or bottom-pressure-head observations. Within this framework, hydraulic states and river discharge can be reconstructed, and bed topography can be inferred when discretized bed-elevation data are available. The unified inverse formulation is implemented in three task-specific configurations for different observation types and bed-information conditions. For prescribed continuous and smooth bed profiles, water-depth or bottom-pressure-head observations are utilized to reconstruct hydraulic states and estimate discharge. When only sparse discretized bed information is available, the framework is extended to simultaneously reconstruct water depth, bottom pressure, bed topography, and discharge within a unified learning process. The proposed approach is evaluated through representative numerical experiments. Results demonstrate that the framework can reliably estimate discharge and reconstruct hydraulic states under limited observation conditions. In scenarios with sparse bed information, the method successfully recovers bed topography while maintaining accurate discharge estimation and consistent hydraulic state reconstruction. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using SGN-constrained physics-informed learning for observation-limited hydrodynamic inversion, discharge estimation, and bed-topography recovery in controlled benchmark cases.

recovered_records.title: Conditional normalizing flows: a generative framework for probabilistic streamflow forecasting
recovered_records.abstract: This study develops an end-to-end probabilistic streamflow forecasting framework that combines a gated recurrent unit (GRU) encoder with a conditional normalizing flow (CNF). Rational quadratic spline transformations are used to learn an explicit conditional streamflow density and generate predictive quantiles within a unified trainable framework. The framework was first evaluated in a one-day-ahead regional experiment using a shared model across Catchment Attributes and Meteorology for Large-sample Studies (CAMELS) catchments and was subsequently examined in a 1- to 4-day case study in the Tunxi catchment. In the CAMELS experiment, the deterministic performance of CNF was comparable to that of the other frameworks, and 92.0% of catchments exceeded both the deterministic-skill and interval-reliability diagnostic thresholds. For CAMELS catchments where test-period high flows exceeded the training-period maxima, CNF remained among the leading frameworks in both deterministic and probabilistic performance. In the Tunxi experiment, CNF achieved the highest deterministic skill at the 1- to 3-day lead times and the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS; 12.189–48.044 m3/s) and highest containing ratio coefficient (CRC; 0.9718–0.9976) across all four lead times. A matched long short-term memory (LSTM) backbone control further showed comparable overall performance between LSTM-CNF and an LSTM-based quantile regression neural network (LSTM-QRNN), with LSTM-CNF showing slight advantages in average point-forecast accuracy and CRC. These results demonstrate that CNF provides an end-to-end optimized, explicit, and flexible conditional-density representation while maintaining predictive performance competitive with the comparison frameworks.

recovered_records.title: Integrated remote sensing retrieval of surface and root-zone soil moisture through physical mechanisms-guided machine learning
recovered_records.abstract: Surface soil moisture (SSM) and root-zone soil moisture (RZSM), as key variables in the water cycle, play a crucial role in regulating water, energy, and carbon exchanges between the land surface and the atmosphere. Currently, satellite remote sensing retrieval technology is widely applied as an effective method for acquiring large-scale SSM data. However, the limited penetration capability of remote sensing signals into the soil presents significant challenges for the retrieval of RZSM. Physical and machine learning (ML) retrieval models require extensive labeled data to achieve high-accuracy retrieval, which poses difficulties in regions with limited in-situ data. To address these challenges, this study proposed an integrated retrieval framework for SSM and RZSM that combines physical mechanisms with ML models. This framework operates in two stages: in the first stage, a radiative transfer model based on brightness temperature data serves as the core, with the ML model employed to optimize the structure and parameters of the physical model, thereby enabling accurate retrieval of SSM. The SSM outputs subsequently serve as direct inputs for the subsequent stage. In the second stage, the ML retrieval model serves as the cornerstone, where the knowledge of soil moisture dynamics informs feature optimization to enable high-accuracy RZSM estimation. The retrieval framework demonstrated strong generalization and spatial extrapolation capabilities in jointly retrieving SSM and RZSM within the validation area in China. The development of this retrieval framework enables high-accuracy soil moisture retrieval in areas with limited monitoring sites, which lays the groundwork for generating large-scale soil moisture products, and provides robust data support for hydrological and climate-related research.

recovered_records.title: A differentiable Xin’anjiang model incorporating transfer learning for cross-basin flood prediction under data scarcity
recovered_records.abstract: In data–scarce basins, hydrological models often fail to capture the peak–dominated, nonstationary behaviour of rainfall–runoff events, limiting cross–basin generalization. To reconcile physical interpretability with deep learning capacity, we develop a differentiable Xin’anjiang model (dXAJ) that couples the conceptual XAJ structure with an LSTM network via differentiable programming, and further integrates transfer learning to enhance regional adaptability. Using 663 flood events from 18 diverse basins in Anhui Province, China, we evaluate dXAJ against the XAJ and LSTM under three tiers: data–rich training, zero–shot ungauged transfer, and fine–tuning with limited local data. Regionally trained dXAJ achieves a median KGE of 0.785 on the test set, rising to 0.811 for large floods, confirming robust temporal generalization. In zero–shot transfer, the multi–source pre–trained dXAJ attains a median KGE of 0.694 and a median absolute peak error of 21.4%, with log–regression R2 > 0.90 for peak flows, demonstrating strong spatial transferability. With transfer learning, fine–tuning using only 33% of local events yields a KGE of 0.785 and reduces peak error to 15%, matching full–data performance, indicating that the primary benefit lies in lowering data demand rather than raising the upper bound. Parameter analysis further shows that transfer–learning corrections align with the natural drift induced by expanded data (84% directional consistency, correlation 0.64), confirming a physically consistent parameter space. These findings demonstrate that differentiable hydrological modelling integrated with transfer learning provides a practical, interpretable framework for improving flood prediction and cross–basin generalization in data–scarce regions.

recovered_records.title: Benchmarking a bounded-coordinate DeepONet for unsaturated flow and solute transport under time-varying infiltration
recovered_records.abstract: Repeated solution of the Richards and advection–dispersion equations can make large-scale ensemble evaluation of unsaturated-flow and solute-transport scenarios computationally restrictive. We evaluate RegShift-DeepONet, a bounded-coordinate variant of Shift-DeepONet that receives a time-varying infiltration hydrograph qtop(t) and soil hydraulic parameters and predicts pressure head h(z,t) and concentration c(z,t). The tanh-bounded affine transform is treated as a guardrail on coordinate adaptation rather than as a hard physical constraint. Five architectures are compared using common data splits, three random seeds, and parity in training budgets under in-distribution (IID), high-peak, and late-peak forcing tests. For the median sample-wise concentration relative L2 error, the bounded model obtains 0.0617±0.0023, 0.0714±0.0081, and 0.0692±0.0096, respectively. The corresponding unconstrained Shift-DeepONet errors are 0.0612±0.0115, 0.0698±0.0136, and 0.0753±0.0158. Thus, their differences under IID and high-peak forcing are smaller than the observed three-seed variability, while bounding reduces concentration error by 8.1% under the late-peak shift. A tuned Fourier neural operator gives errors of 0.1184−−0.1305. Supplementary temporal-shape and joint forcing–soil stress tests delineate the conditions under which process-model confirmation is required. Mass-balance error is used as a conservative trigger for HYDRUS review rather than as a stand-alone accuracy certificate. The results support a focused conclusion: bounded coordinate adaptation can selectively stabilise temporal extrapolation, with applicability checks and HYDRUS confirmation providing an auditable screening workflow.

recovered_records.title: TS-PINN: a dual-branch physics-informed neural network based on two-source theory for evapotranspiration estimation
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate estimation of surface energy fluxes and evapotranspiration (ET) is essential for understanding land–atmosphere interactions. While data-driven methods efficiently fit observations, their “black-box” nature makes it challenging to guarantee physical interpretability and reliable extrapolation from instantaneous to daily ET. To address these limitations, we propose the Two-Source Physics-Informed Neural Network (TS-PINN), driven by both physical structure and physical constraints. The model constructs a vegetation–soil dual-branch architecture structurally aligned with the Two-Source Energy Balance (TSEB) theory, embedding partitioning mechanisms as structural inductive biases. For optimization, we design a multi-constraint physical loss that integrates instantaneous energy balance, component energy balance, the Priestley–Taylor (P–T) upper bound, and daily-scale consistency. We also adopt an adaptive weighting strategy to balance data fitting and physical consistency. Validation against eddy covariance (EC) data in the Heihe River Basin (HRB) (2015–2021 growing seasons) shows that TS-PINN significantly outperforms Random Forest (RF) and Deep Neural Network (DNN) baselines. Its root mean square error (RMSE) values are 31.22 W/m2 for sensible heat flux (H) and 44.03 W/m2 for latent heat flux (LE), with corresponding coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.79 and 0.85, respectively. Ablation experiments reveal that the structural inductive bias enhances component-level representation, while the physical loss terms effectively constrain prediction boundaries. Specifically, the instantaneous energy balance constraint dominates H prediction accuracy, and the P–T constraint guides LE estimation. Daily ET converted from LE also presents good consistency with observations, with a Kling-Gupta Efficiency (KGE) of 0.88 and an R2 of 0.81. Overall, TS-PINN offers a novel, accurate, and physically interpretable approach for simulating surface energy fluxes and ET.

recovered_records.title: A dependency-guided symbolic regression framework for overcoming error compensation in hybrid AI–physical models
recovered_records.abstract: Integrating AI-discovered formulas into process-based Earth system models is difficult. Earth functions as a connected system with directional dependencies from upstream to downstream. When components are trained in isolation and later embedded, error compensation can occur: downstream modules absorb upstream errors, local metrics appear strong, yet system performance and physical consistency decline. We use hydrologic modeling as a tractable testbed. Deep symbolic regression (DSR) provides transparent evapotranspiration (ET) formulas. A knowledge guided variant (KG-DSR) builds runoff relations that preserve links among surface runoff, interflow, and baseflow. These expressions are first trained and evaluated with observed meteorology, then inserted into the HBV model under several integration strategies, including a sequential scheme that stabilizes ET before calibrating runoff. ET formulas from DSR outperform the original HBV scheme in offline tests. More than 70% of basins show higher Kling–Gupta efficiency (KGE) and lower RMSE, with better representation of vegetation controls on ET. In coupled runs, adding only the ET module yields limited benefit. The sequential strategy improves system behavior: relative to embedding runoff alone, ET KGE rises by 16.1% and streamflow KGE by 4.9%; relative to the HBV baseline, gains reach 11.6% and 10.1%. Performance for extreme flows and baseflow indicators is also highest under the sequential strategy. Stabilizing upstream ET reduces error compensation and strengthens cross-process consistency in coupled hydrologic models. A stepwise inclusion of explicit, interpretable parameters offers a general path to transparent, AI-guided modeling of complex Earth system processes, with implications for drought forecasting, flood risk assessment, and low flow management.

recovered_records.title: An orthogonal residual physics-informed neural network with Karhunen-Loève expansion for inversion of heterogeneous soil hydraulic parameters
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate inversion of heterogeneous soil hydraulic parameters is essential but ill-posed owing to nonlinear flow physics, coupled van Genuchten-Mualem (VGM) parameters, and incomplete boundary information. The Karhunen-Loève expansion (KLE) provides a useful geostatistical prior, but accurate priors are rarely available. Deep neural networks (DNNs) add flexibility, yet naive DNN-KLE coupling in physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can create representational conflicts when the DNN overlaps the KLE subspace. We propose an orthogonal-residual KLE-PINN that separates prior-supported modes from neural residual components through an orthogonal projection. In controlled one-dimensional experiments, we benchmark the method for joint inversion of heterogeneous VGM parameters under an uncertain-boundary setting against unified and decoupled PINNs, a standard KLE-PINN, and a naive additive hybrid. Shared-output DNNs reproduce hydraulic states well but recover parameter fields poorly, whereas parameter-specific subnetworks only partly reduce this limitation. Under accurate priors, the additive hybrid degrades valid KLE solutions because its components compete for overlapping modes. Under biased priors, variance errors are mostly absorbed by coefficient rescaling, whereas correlation-length errors cause stronger structural bias and cross-parameter compensation. Overall, the proposed model achieves the most accurate and robust parameter reconstructions across tested prior settings by preserving prior-supported modes and assigning DNN flexibility to complementary structures. These results show that robust hybrid PINN inversion requires explicit separation of prior-supported modes and neural residual components.

recovered_records.title: An attention-enhanced hybrid physics-informed neural network for multi-parameter inversion of heterogeneous reservoirs in CO2 geological storage
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate characterization of heterogeneous reservoir properties and robust prediction of CO2 plume migration are critical for the safety assessment and monitoring of geological carbon storage. Geological parameter inversion in high-dimensional heterogeneous reservoirs under limited observations remains a strongly ill-posed problem. In this study, an attention-enhanced hybrid physics-informed neural network inversion framework is developed. This framework integrates multiphase flow governing equations, rock-physics constraints, observational data, low-dimensional geological priors, and attention-enhanced neural-network representations into a unified inversion architecture and loss formulation. A hybrid attention mechanism combining parallel sub-networks, self-attention, and cross-attention is designed to improve the network’s ability to learn complex nonlinear features. Karhunen-Loève expansion (KLE) is employed to construct a low-dimensional and geologically constrained prior parameter representation. Gaussian kernel feature mapping is also used to improve the caption of localized variations. The proposed framework is validated using a two-dimensional single-well CO2 injection scenario in a heterogeneous reservoir. Numerical results demonstrate that the framework can accurately reconstruct pressure and saturation fields, as well as heterogeneous distributions of porosity and permeability. A systematic ablation study further confirms the critical roles of attention mechanisms and KLE-based prior representations in improving inversion accuracy and stability. This study provides a promising tool for prediction and risk assessment in CO2 geological storage applications.

recovered_records.title: Decoupling geogenic and anthropogenic drivers of groundwater natural background levels using machine learning and high-resolution maps
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate determination of natural background levels (NBLs) of groundwater hydrochemistry is critical for setting water quality standards, yet traditional approaches often fail to capture spatial heterogeneity, particularly in large-scale regions with uneven monitoring networks and human activities. To bridge the gap, this study proposes a novel framework that integrates machine learning models (TabPFN and XGBoost) with spatial grid resampling to model NBLs and their controlling factors (strata, land use/land cover, topographic slope, population, and nitrogen fertilizer use), thereby generating high-resolution NBL maps. A total of 1250 groundwater samples from the northwest Sichuan Basin, China, were used to validate this framework. The results showed that TabPFN outperformed XGBoost in NBL prediction across all parameters, yielding higher R2 (0.933–0.979) and reduced uncertainty by 15%–44%. The high-resolution NBL maps revealed that, although lithology remained the primary control on geogenic indicators (e.g., Ca2+, Mg2+), anthropogenic drivers reshaped the baseline patterns of hydrochemical parameters (e.g., NO3-N, Cl−, and Na+). The dissolution of mirabilite, dolomitic strata (Cretaceous), and calcareous formations (Jurassic) explained the elevated SO42−/Na+ in the groundwater environmental unit (GEU) Ⅰ, Mg2+ in GEU Ⅱ, and Ca2+ in GEUs Ⅲ–Ⅵ, respectively. Slow groundwater runoff increased hydrochemical concentration in GEUs Ⅰ and Ⅲ–Ⅵ. Domestic sewage and nitrogen fertilizer application were identified as the primary sources of elevated Na+/Cl− and NO3-N levels, respectively, which notably affected GEUs Ⅰ and Ⅲ–Ⅴ. The maps characterized the spatial heterogeneity of NBLs, thereby enhancing the understanding of baseline hydrochemistry. Contemporary NBL should be regarded as a present-day baseline modified by modern human activities. These findings provide an effective approach for determining groundwater NBLs across large, unevenly sampled areas.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed operator learning for rapid hydrograph-to-field prediction on an unstructured-mesh flood benchmark
recovered_records.abstract: Rapid two-dimensional flood surrogate modeling requires fast full-field evaluation when many forcing scenarios must be screened, yet high-resolution shallow-water solvers remain computationally expensive in many-query settings. Here we develop a physics-informed Deep Operator Network (PI-DeepONet) for fixed-domain hydrograph-to-field prediction on a high-resolution unstructured-mesh flood benchmark. The model learns a mapping from upstream inflow hydrographs to spatiotemporal water-depth and velocity fields while incorporating reduced shallow-water-equation residuals as soft regularization terms during training. The benchmark reference fields are generated using HEC-RAS v6.6 simulations over a 9.27 km2 sub-basin of the Qingshui River Basin, China, discretized with 91,959 unstructured cells. Relative to an architecture-matched data-driven DeepONet baseline, PI-DeepONet reduces localized errors near wet–dry fronts, mitigates non-physical leakage, and shows improved transient routing behavior under the evaluated steady and unsteady benchmark conditions. Under the withheld extreme event, the model also shows improved RVF behavior and lower event-scale volume error relative to the baseline. After offline training, GPU-accelerated inference requires only seconds, corresponding to approximately three orders of magnitude faster online evaluation than CPU-based HEC-RAS in the present setup. Tests on identical CPU hardware also indicate an algorithmic speed-up of more than two orders of magnitude. These results support physics-regularized operator learning as a viable benchmark-specific surrogate strategy for rapid multi-scenario screening under fixed-domain flood-model settings.

recovered_records.title: Coupled hydrological and public health risks from urban flooding: integrated remote sensing, machine learning, and hydrodynamic–ecological modelling
recovered_records.abstract: Urban flooding poses concurrent threats to infrastructure, human safety, and public health, particularly in densely populated megacities around the globe, where floodwater often acts as a mobile pathway for microbial contamination. This study develops an integrated remote sensing–machine learning–hydrodynamic modelling framework to quantify coupled flood and microbial health risks. Water surface temperature retrieved from Landsat thermal infrared imagery was used as a predictor in a Support Vector Regression model to estimate spatio-temporal variations in E. coli concentration. These predicted microbial loads were subsequently incorporated into a 3-way coupled MIKE + Flood–ECO Lab framework to simulate flood inundation, contaminant transport, and exposure pathways under flood conditions. Hydro-meteorological forcings, including rainfall, streamflow, and urban drainage flow, together with spatial inputs such as topography and land use–land cover, were used to drive the hydrodynamic simulations. The predicted E. coli concentrations were used to parameterize microbial loading, and infection risks for adults and children exposed to contaminated floodwater were quantified using the β-Poisson dose–response model. Experimenting with the proposed framework over Delhi (India)- a city highly prone to flooding and waterborne health hazards, reveals that ∼ 63% of floodplains faced “high” to “very high” flood hazards, with E. coli levels consistently exceeding safe bathing thresholds (500 MPN/100 mL). Estimated annual infection risks surpassed the USEPA benchmark, with children being the most vulnerable. The study provides actionable recommendations for holistic flood management and emphasizes the urgent need to integrate microbial water quality into flood risk assessment and public health planning, particularly in rapidly urbanizing, climate-sensitive regions.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed machine learning of hyporheic exchange driven by channel blockage and riverbed morphodynamics
recovered_records.abstract: Riverbed morphodynamic alterations induced by channel blockages, particularly those associated with large woody debris (LWD), play a critical role in modulating hyporheic exchange processes. However, most existing predictive approaches have not fully accounted for scour–deposition evolution, limiting the accuracy of hyporheic exchange flux (HEF) estimation. To address this, our study develops an enhanced physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework to quantify the combined effects of hydraulic conditions, structural configuration, and riverbed morphology on hyporheic exchange dynamics. The computational framework generates 97 synthetic LWD-flow interaction cases, with six representative morphodynamic descriptors extracted to parameterize the resultant scour–deposition architecture. HEF was predicted through a hierarchical framework integrating empirical regressions, machine learning, and PIML, enabling adaptive estimation under varying data conditions. With morphodynamic descriptors available, both the empirical equation and ensemble learning models reproduced HEF with high accuracy (NSE ≈ 0.96); whereas using only initial flow–structure inputs reduced accuracy and the PIML approach, which incorporates the study-derived empirical flux equation, maintained higher performance (NSE = 0.79). SHAP analysis revealed that HEF is primarily governed by flow–morphology interactions and effective submergence ratio. Ensemble-based models, particularly Extra Trees and Gradient Boosting, demonstrated high predictive skill in capturing nonlinear morphodynamic responses. These results demonstrate that the hierarchical framework provides a unified and physically consistent strategy for predicting HEF across variable hydraulic–morphologic conditions.

recovered_records.title: The application of geospatially-integrated machine learning models for flood prediction: A review
recovered_records.abstract: With the increase in flooding events globally, Artificial Intelligence (AI) approaches, particularly geospatially integrated machine learning (ML), have emerged as a viable tool for flood modeling. This review systematically analyzed 100 peer-reviewed articles published between 1990 and 2024 to examine trends in ML applications across different flood types, their performance, opportunities, and limitations, and to identify gaps between research activity and flood occurrence, highlighting the need for capacity building in some regions. Results show that ML models are most frequently applied to pluvial floods (44%), followed by fluvial (40%), compound (9%), and coastal (7%) floods, while applications for pluvial, coastal, and compound flooding continue to increase. ANN-based models were the most commonly applied approaches, particularly in fluvial and compound flood studies, followed by SVM and RF models. Reported model performance varied substantially across studies depending on flood type, data availability, and validation strategy, with several localized studies reporting very high predictive accuracy under controlled validation conditions. The geographical distribution of 2,395 flood occurrences from the EM-DAT database revealed disparities between research output and flood occurrence. Publications align relatively well with Asia (50% of publications; 1,450 flood events), Europe (22%; 336 events), and North America (17%; 207 events), whereas Africa (5%; 97 events) and South America (5%; 244 events) remain underrepresented despite significant flood exposure. These findings highlight the need for improved data access, capacity building, and transferable ML approaches to support flood prediction research in underrepresented but flood-prone regions.

recovered_records.title: Seasonal controls, recharge thresholds, and hydrological memory in karst groundwater dynamics revealed by interpretable deep learning
recovered_records.abstract: Quantifying groundwater responses to climate forcing in karst systems remains difficult because recharge is nonlinear, threshold-dependent, and modulated by antecedent storage. We developed an interpretable deep learning framework to diagnose seasonal controls, threshold-like recharge behavior, and hydrological memory in the Baotu Spring karst watershed of northern China. A 66-year groundwater-level (GWL) record was segmented to isolate the period primarily controlled by meteorological forcing. Daily precipitation (P) and temperature (T) data from 2012 to 2024 were then used to train a long short-term memory model, and Expected Gradients together with Additive Decomposition quantified driver contributions and temporal memory. The model accurately reproduced groundwater dynamics in independent testing (Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) = 0.93, coefficient of determination (R2) = 0.95, and root mean square error (RMSE) = 0.155 m). Attribution analysis revealed a clear seasonal hierarchy: summer exerted the strongest model-attributed control on groundwater variability, whereas autumn contributed secondarily through delayed recharge transmission. At the annual scale, P attributions became more positive when annual P exceeded 620 mm and GWLs were above 28.5 m, suggesting a threshold-like shift toward stronger positive model-attributed GWL sensitivity. At the event scale, the strongest positive P-related attribution occurred for daily P of 11.4–41.3 mm; smaller events were consistent with vadose-zone replenishment, whereas larger events suggested reduced marginal recharge efficiency due to greater runoff partitioning. High-GWL events were dominated by rainfall forcing, with short memory in summer, whereas winter rainfall memory extended to approximately five months; low-GWL events were linked to persistent P deficits, elevated T, and unfavorable rainfall-intensity distributions. These model-derived indicators support recharge assessment and groundwater-drought early warning in heterogeneous karst systems.

recovered_records.title: Deep learning-enhanced sequential updating of hydraulic parameters and state variables in groundwater models
recovered_records.abstract: As a fundamental component of the hydrological cycle, groundwater systems play a critical role in sustaining ecosystems, securing water resources, and supporting socio-economic development. However, substantial uncertainties remain in both parameter estimation and state prediction, limiting the reliability of groundwater models. Improving predictive accuracy therefore requires the sequential, real-time updating of model states and parameters using newly acquired observations. Although the ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) has been widely applied for this purpose, its performance can degrade in non-Gaussian and strongly nonlinear systems, for which approaches based on transformations or multiple-point geostatistics have been proposed as effective remedies. In this study, we present an alternative strategy by introducing a deep learning (DL)-based update strategy into the EnKF framework, resulting in a hybrid ensemble filtering approach that integrates DL-based nonlinear updates with Kalman-type linear updates, termed EF(DL-K). The proposed method is designed to more effectively fuse information from numerical models and observations in complex groundwater systems. Compared with the conventional EnKF and a purely DL-based ensemble filter [EF(DL)], EF(DL-K) exhibits enhanced flexibility and robustness in the sequential updating of both hydraulic parameters and state variables in subsurface aquifer systems. The impact of the placement of the DL step within the EF(DL-K) framework is systematically investigated. The results show that EF(DL-K) yields assimilation performance comparable to that of the EnKF under Gaussian conditions, while achieving substantially improved joint state-parameter estimation under non-Gaussian conditions. Overall, EF(DL-K) provides a promising filtering-based data assimilation framework for real-time model-data integration and the dynamic updating of both parameters and state variables in groundwater systems.

recovered_records.title: Simulation of pollutant transport and identification of longitudinal dispersion coefficient in vegetated channels based on a vegetation-constrained physics-informed neural network
recovered_records.abstract: The longitudinal dispersion coefficient Dx is a key parameter in the advection–dispersion equation and directly influences the accuracy of pollutant-transport simulations in rivers. Empirical formulas currently used to predict Dx often yield widely varying results and lack general applicability, particularly under complex hydraulic conditions. In vegetated channels, aquatic vegetation produces pronounced lateral shear and heterogeneous velocity fields, which makes the prediction of Dx a challenging task. A vegetation-constrained physics-informed neural network (V-PINN) is developed to predict Dx by embedding a zonal vegetation model into the physical constraints of the learning process. Training on datasets covering multiple vegetation types and flow regimes enables V-PINN to capture vegetation-induced mixing processes and to predict Dx with Relative Error (RE) below 0.233 under sparse or missing data. The proposed V-PINN exhibits superior performance over both the traditional N-zone formula and the standard PINN in estimating Dx. The standard PINN achieves reliable prediction of Dx and prediction of pollutant transport in natural rivers. The predicted Dx is integrated into a two-dimensional PINN in natural rivers to simulate pollutant transport, with RE below 0.064, demonstrating improved alignment with measured data and enhanced applicability in real rivers. The standard PINN also achieves reliable prediction of Dx and pollutant transport in natural rivers. The proposed V-PINN framework provides physically consistent predictions across diverse vegetation conditions and demonstrates the potential of physics-informed deep learning as an accurate and interpretable extension of classical hydraulic theory for modeling vegetation–flow interactions.

recovered_records.title: Multicomponent geochemical reactions control arsenic mobilization in groundwater: novel insights from machine learning and geochemical model
recovered_records.abstract: Redox sensitive elements, including carbon (C), nitrogen (N), sulfur (S), iron (Fe), and manganese (Mn), play critical roles in groundwater arsenic (As) cycling. However, the behavior of As under the simultaneous influence of multiple interacting geochemical cycles remains poorly understood. In this study, self-organizing maps (SOM) and absolute principal component scores-multiple linear regression (APCS-MLR) were applied to identify the dominant mechanisms controlling As mobilization and transformation in groundwater. Based on these analyses, a multicomponent inverse geochemical model (MC-IGM) was developed for the Hasuhai Basin, China to elucidate coupled C-N-S-Fe-Mn-As cycling in groundwater. Integrated PCA-APCS-SOM analysis further identified four dominant factors controlling geogenic As contamination in groundwater, including geogenic sources (30.75%), Fe/Mn oxide redox transformations and anthropogenic inputs (35.63%), evaporative processes (0.97%), and water–rock interactions (32.66%). Geochemical modeling indicates that the redox cycles of Fe/Mn oxides govern the interconversion between As(III)/As(V). Heterotrophic dissimilatory NO3− reduction to NH4+ (h-DNRA), organic nitrogen (Org-N) mineralization, sulfate reduction, and methanogenesis promote the enrichment of As. In contrast, nitrification enhanced As adsorption through coupling with Fe/Mn oxidation process. Collectively, these findings identify carbon cycling as the central process coupling N, S, Fe, and Mn transformations, ultimately controlling As mobility and speciation.

recovered_records.title: Parameterized physics-informed neural networks for flow reconstruction around idealized islands under data-sparse conditions
recovered_records.abstract: Sustainable management of coastal island environments is often hampered by limited observational data and the high computational cost of resolving complex flow dynamics. This research introduces a parameterized physics–informed neural network (PINN) framework that integrates experimental measurements with flow physics to reconstruct three-dimensional flow fields around islands. The methodology employs a multi-stage training approach: initial learning from domain-wide large eddy simulations, followed by refinement using tomographic particle image velocimetry data, and final optimization across multiple flow regimes. Validation against independent experimental datasets demonstrates robust performance across Reynolds numbers 24,000–96,000, achieving correlation coefficients exceeding 0.9 for primary flow components. Crucially, the framework successfully infers flow characteristics in unmeasured regions, particularly near‑bed zones essential for assessing erosion processes and benthic habitat stability. Analysis reveals complex, regime-dependent relationships between hydrological parameters and wake dynamics that traditional discrete sampling cannot resolve. Specifically, the model identifies an optimal eco-hydrological stability window at intermediate Reynolds numbers (Re≈48,000), driven by a stable wake reattachment mechanism that shelters downstream habitats. Furthermore, it quantifies a distinct thrust generation window and significant low-Re flow asymmetry, providing critical insights for sediment transport pathways. The trained model enables rapid generation of: (i) eco-hydrological suitability maps for marine spatial planning, (ii) erosion risk assessments based on bed shear stress distributions, and (iii) hydraulic resistance characterizations for regional scale modeling. This approach offers significant advantages for coastal hydrology by providing high-fidelity field reconstruction from experimental data, offering a valuable tool for water resource management and environmental protection in complex island systems.

Evaluated on a 3D random-field heterogeneity case, the framework achieves a head RMSE of 3.61 m (R2 = 0.896) and a concentration RMSE of 1.02 mg/L (R2 = 0.864). Furthermore, two-stage training proved essential for concentration accuracy, preventing error propagation from velocity fields. recovered_records.title: Quantifying heterogeneous hydrological interactions in complex river basins: an interpretable spatiotemporal deep learning approach
recovered_records.abstract: Hydrological regimes in complex river basins are governed by heterogeneous hydrological interactions, including driver-to-response interactions induced by multi-source inflows and response-to-response interactions within basin-scale hydrological processes. These interactions are essential for guiding scientific river-basin regulation, while their systematic quantification remains challenging, constrained by computation-intensive modeling and scenario-limited analysis. To this end, this study develops an Interpretable Spatio-Temporal Hydrological Interaction Learning (InSTIL) framework, which combines LSTM-based temporal encoding, graph-based spatial propagating and Shapley Additive Explanations, to explicitly capture and quantify the hydrological interactions. Applied to the Three Gorges Reservoir (TGR) and Dongting Lake (DTL) system, InSTIL delivers robust simulations of lake water levels with an average RMSE of 0.425 m, consistently outperforming LSTM and GCN benchmarks, particularly under extreme conditions. Furthermore, interaction interpretation reveals that: (1) For driver-to-response interactions between rivers and the lake, their spatial patterns from different rivers are governed by inflow locations and runoff volumes, with TGR releases exerting the dominant influence (contributing 32.89%-48.58% across individual sites) and tributary Yuan River ranking second. Meanwhile, these interactions appear unimodal over time, showing the strongest daily impacts at 1–3 days before lake’s responses. Their multi-day cumulative effects inform an effective regulation window of 7–15 days. (2) For response-to-response interactions within the lake, the heterogeneous response timing and magnitude across DTL reveal the weak hydraulic connectivity in the south sub-lake and the presence of a cross-sublake hydraulic pathway. Overall, InSTIL provides a transferable paradigm for robust hydrological simulations and systematic interaction interpretation, offering practical insights for sustainable river-basin management.

recovered_records.title: A physics-guided and interpretable machine learning framework for rapid flood inundation mapping in complex flood retention areas
recovered_records.abstract: Rapid and accurate flood mapping using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery is a critical tool for emergency response. While machine learning (ML) models have significantly enhanced the accuracy and efficiency of flood mapping, their “black box” nature limits their trustworthiness for critical emergency response applications. To address this issue, we developed an interpretable flood mapping framework based on Gaofen-3 (GF-3) SAR imagery that fuses remote sensing physics with data-driven analysis. The framework comprises three core components: (1) a novel physics-guided feature, the Generalized Normalized Difference Polarization Index (GNDPI), which transforms skewed backscatter data into a more separable bimodal distribution; (2) a Random Forest (RF) classification model incorporating multi-source features, including Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM), Local Binary Pattern (LBP), and Haar Wavelet; and (3) the SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) method, utilized to interpret the model’s decisions. The framework was successfully applied to the Dongdian flood retention area (DFRA) during China’s “23·7″ major flood event, yielding high accuracy (Overall Accuracy (OA) = 97.72%, Kappa = 0.953). In model comparisons, the RF model demonstrated over four times the computational efficiency of XGBoost, with a minimal 0.11% loss in accuracy, proving its practical value for emergency scenarios. Crucially, SHAP analysis revealed that the model learned a physically consistent decision logic, prioritizing features for macroscopic smoothness and microscopic uniformity, and leveraging complex feature interactions to differentiate water from non-water pixels. This study’s framework not only improves flood mapping performance but also demystifies the model’s decision logic via SHAP, offering a transparent and robust tool for rapid emergency response in data-scarce basins.

recovered_records.title: Temporal inductive biases in hourly flood forecasting: a comparative analysis of recurrent, attention-based, and state-space neural networks
recovered_records.abstract: Daily-resolution flood forecasts often encounter difficulties in capturing rapid runoff fluctuations over short time periods. To address this limitation, moving to hourly-scale modeling is essential, yet identifying which deep learning architectures possess the optimal temporal inductive biases for such high-frequency dynamics remains an open challenge. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of recurrent, attention-based, and state-space neural networks, benchmarked against simple layered structures on discharge-assisted forecasting tasks across 516 CAMELS catchments. The results indicate that the Patch Transformer achieves the best predictive performance. This suggests that patch-based processing acts as a superior inductive bias by smoothing high-frequency noise and extracting local temporal semantics, which effectively captures long-term routing and hydrological dependencies better than point-wise attention. While the traditional LSTM maintains robust performance, the Mamba model demonstrates a promising balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Furthermore, through an interpretability analysis combining attention weights with Integrated Gradients (IG), we reveal that attention models successfully capture physical hydrological patterns, such as time-lagged responses and the dominance of dynamic meteorological drivers over static attributes. This work offers theoretical insights into how architectural choices determine short-term forecasting capability under diverse hydro-climatic regimes.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed gated transformer for robust flash flood forecasting in data-scarce small catchments via variance-constrained learning
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate operational flash flood forecasting in small, data-scarce catchments remains a persistent challenge due to sparse monitoring networks, severe spatial scale mismatches, and highly noisy input data. This study proposes a Physics-Informed Gated Transformer with Variance-Constrained Learning. In contrast to hard-constrained Physics-Informed Neural Networks, this framework utilizes hydrological mechanisms as soft inductive biases. First, it integrates a causally-strict, leakage-free baseflow separation and saturation-excess effective rainfall to physically constrain the solution space. Second, a Gated Residual Network is deployed to dynamically filter high-frequency noise from multi-source inputs. Third, a variance-constrained multi-step loss function is mathematically formulated to explicitly penalize the attenuation of flood peaks. Application in the highly flashy Guanshan River Basin demonstrates that the proposed architecture achieves competitive forecasting accuracy at a 1-hour lead time, effectively mitigating systemic phase-lag and performing favorably against strictly recalibrated baselines including HBV (NSE = −0.044) and standard LSTM (NSE = 0.315). The GRN preserves stable predictive accuracy even under 80% synthetic noise injection. Furthermore, Explainable AI attribution via Gradient SHAP empirically indicates that the network handles spatial scale mismatch by deploying coarse ERA5 data primarily as an antecedent moisture “macro-state proxy”. Finally, zero-shot spatial generalization testing on twelve climatically-matched small forested basins drawn from the CAMELS-US dataset shows that the proposed architecture maintains performance comparable to two state-of-the-art large-sample benchmarks and significantly outperforms a Vanilla Transformer counterpart. These findings highlight that coupling soft physical inductive biases with gated architectures offers a transferable, physics-constrained framework for operational early warning in poorly gauged catchments.

recovered_records.title: Neural operator-based multi-objective optimization for spatiotemporal data-informed seepage parameter identification: a case study on deep overburden in a dam foundation

Time-varying water levels and spatially distributed (left bank, riverbed, and right bank) monitoring data from multiple seepage-pressure points are fused into a unified multi-objective formulation. DeepONet is conditioned on physics-informed spatial descriptors, enabling operator learning of the mapping from seepage parameters to spatiotemporal pressure responses, and achieving high prediction fidelity (R2 = 0.994–0.999). The optimization efficiency of IMOCOA is enhanced by the Sobol initialization, dynamic β-η learning, and ε-dominance-based truncation, achieving a low inverted generational distance (0.109) and a high hypervolume (0.539). The framework is validated on a rockfill dam founded on deep overburden with a thickness of 148 m, and the identified parameters reproduce observed seepage-pressure evolution and yield physically consistent seepage behavior. Comparative analyses demonstrate that the framework achieves higher computational efficiency and robustness for seepage parameter identification by explicitly integrating domain-specific physical information, demonstrating its potential for broader application in complex geotechnical and hydraulic engineering problems.

recovered_records.title: Process guided graph-based transformer learning for streamflow predictions in data-sparse river basins
recovered_records.abstract: Streamflow prediction in data-sparse regions has traditionally relied on process-based hydrological models (PBMs) or hybrid approaches that combine physical modeling with data-driven learning. However, these methods typically require extensive calibration using local observations and detailed knowledge of internal model parameters, which limits their transferability and interpretability when applied to ungauged basins. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel Process-Guided Graph–Transformer (PGT) framework that surrogates PBMs and enhances streamflow prediction in ungauged basins (PUB) using uncalibrated PBM parameters without explicit calibration or optimization. The proposed framework integrates uncalibrated PBM outputs, river network topology, Graph Neural Networks, and Transformers for spatio-temporal learning, and is evaluated across three hydrologically contrasting river basins in India, Australia, and the United States. Results show that PGT consistently improves predictive skill, increasing median KGE from −0.5 to 0.4 for baseline models (SWAT and SWAT-SUFI2) to 0.50–0.75, while maintaining PBIAS within ± 10%, compared with baseline overprediction frequently exceeding 50%. PUB generalization experiments further demonstrate robust skill transfer from gauged to ungauged subbasins, with ΔKGE remaining near 0.0 ± 0.2 across hydrological distances of 0–300 km. Additional analyses indicate improved extreme-event detection (Critical Success Index ≈ 0.8–0.9 compared to 0.4–0.6 for baselines), reliable uncertainty characterization (p-factor: 0.5–1.0 compared to 0.25–0.6 for baselines), and an 8–40 × reduction in computational cost relative to traditional calibration-based approach (SWAT-SUFI2). Overall, these results demonstrate that PGT provides a scalable and process-consistent solution for multi-site streamflow prediction in data-sparse and ungauged regions.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed dual-modal decomposition and deep hybrid learning with interpretability for reliable prediction of dissolved oxygen in complex riverine systems
recovered_records.abstract: Dissolved oxygen (DO) is a critical indicator of riverine aquatic ecosystem health, making high-precision DO forecasting models indispensable for watershed water quality risk early warning and water resource security. Existing methodologies, however, predominantly rely on historical data for water quality simulation, often overlooking inherent physical biases, limited non-linear data processing capabilities, inadequate coupling of long- and short-term dependencies, and empirical parameter reliance. To address these deficiencies, this study first constructs a four-dimensional feature system integrating target, surrounding, and upstream monitoring indicators along with meteorological factors. Subsequently, based on the one-dimensional convection–diffusion-reaction equation for riverine DO, we derive Péclet and two types of Damköhler numbers as core physical prior parameters to incorporate into the model. We next adopt a dual-modal decomposition approach − combining Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) and Complementary Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN) − to separate the long-term evolutionary patterns and short-term dynamic variations in the dataset. Furthermore, an Improved Dung Beetle Optimizer (IDBO) is introduced to optimize VMD decomposition parameters and Bidirectional Temporal Convolutional Network (BiTCN) hyperparameters. Finally, by integrating the physicochemical interaction mechanisms of water temperature, permanganate index, and DO, we refine the loss function to construct the IDBO-VCEEMDAN-TiTransformer-PDL model, which leverages BiTCN and Improved Transformer (iTransformer) for efficient fusion of long- and short-term data features. Experimental results demonstrate the model’s superior predictive performance, with coefficient of determination (R2) values exceeding 0.99 across six upstream and downstream monitoring stations. Notably, the Wolongsi Bridge station achieved an R2 of 0.9989, while the Shawangdu station exhibited remarkably low root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0660 and 0.0533, respectively, far outperforming benchmark comparison models. Experiments confirm that the integration of physical prior mechanisms contributes most significantly to model performance enhancement, accounting for 4.62%, with two-modal decomposition and IDBO hyperparameter optimization yielding improvements of 4.07% and 2.93%, respectively. This model retains the computational efficiency of data-driven approaches while ensuring prediction accuracy and generalizability through physical mechanism constraints, offering a robust technical solution for precise riverine DO concentration forecasting and refined watershed water environment management.

recovered_records.title: Towards more accurate streamflow and flood prediction via explainable CNN-LSTM: leveraging ERA5 gridded precipitation and hydrological observations through input-architecture co-design
recovered_records.abstract: Deep learning has achieved high accuracy in hydrological and hydrodynamic modeling, yet effectively incorporating ungauged, precipitation-driven lateral small tributaries into model architectures for more accurate streamflow prediction remains underexplored. This challenge is particularly pronounced under spatially heterogeneous rainfall, where dimensional mismatches between gridded precipitation data and sparse upstream observations hinder accurate source-sink representation. Here, we propose an integrated framework that combines a three-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN) with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, enabling flexible fusion of gridded precipitation (e.g., ERA5) and upstream hydrological observations. The proposed 3D-CNN-LSTM model incorporating richer spatiotemporal precipitation information yields more accurate and stable streamflow and flood predictions across most stations compared to models using only upstream streamflow and spatially averaged precipitation. Even where precipitation-driven tributary inflows account for as little as 5% of downstream flow, the model improves flood prediction in 80% of events relative to a streamflow-only LSTM. When such tributary inflows contribute positively to downstream streamflow, incorporating spatially distributed precipitation through the 3D-CNN-LSTM leads to improved predictions, even under complex river–lake interactions. In contrast, when precipitation acts as irrelevant or uninformative inputs (e.g., under flow diversion with complex routing pathways), the streamflow-only LSTM architecture performs adequately without the added precipitation noise. Explainable deep learning techniques further provide diagnostic insights into the 3D-CNN-LSTM model’s sensitivity to lagged upstream inputs and reveal patterns that are broadly consistent with known hydrological behavior. This integrated input-architecture co-design strengthens deep learning’s capacity to uncover and interpret streamflow generation mechanisms.

recovered_records.title: Daily inference of reservoir surface water area at large scales via a systematic deep learning framework synergistically integrating multisource remote sensing imagery
recovered_records.abstract: Reservoir surface water area (SWA) serves as a pivotal indicator for characterizing storage changes and water balance, with important implications for assessing the effects of anthropogenic regulation and protecting aquatic ecosystems. Although satellite observations offer indispensable data support for reservoir SWA monitoring, the trade-off between spatial and temporal resolutions in single-source satellite datasets severely impedes the comprehensive quantification of rapid SWA dynamics. To address this challenge, we develop a systematic deep learning framework for daily SWA inference that synergistically combines cloud-free optical image reconstruction and surface water extraction. The reconstruction module generates daily cloud-free Landsat-like optical images by fusing heterogeneous data from Sentinel-1, MODIS, and Landsat-derived NDVI via a multi-branch feature fusion mechanism. Using the reconstructed imagery as input, the surface water extraction module accurately delineates reservoir SWA. Comparative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves robust performance in cloud-free image reconstruction (RMSE = 0.021, SSIM = 0.737) and high accuracy in water extraction, with both user’s and producer’s accuracies exceeding 0.970. The framework is applied to 288 large reservoirs across the Yangtze River Basin, and its scalability for large-scale inference is further validated using in situ water elevation measurements from 77 reservoirs. Overall, this framework provides a robust and scalable solution for daily large-scale reservoir SWA inference, laying a solid foundation for hydrological analysis, optimal reservoir operation, and sustainable water resource management.
