recovered_records.title: A two-layer safe reinforcement learning framework for multi-constraint reservoir operation: Integrating action masking and lagrangian dual method
recovered_records.abstract: Reservoir operation is a safety-critical sequential decision problem that must balance multiple operational objectives under strict water-level and release constraints. However, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms frequently violate safety constraints during exploration, limiting their applicability in real-world engineering. This study proposes a two-layer Safe Reinforcement Learning (SafeRL) framework. The first layer is a state-driven action mask that filters infeasible actions before policy sampling; the second layer is a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-Lagrangian implementation that adaptively adjusts the constraint multiplier to balance safety and performance. Unlike single-mechanism approaches that rely solely on post-hoc correction or fixed penalties, this design combines proactive filtering with adaptive optimization. Additionally, a non-linear action mapping is introduced to improve learning efficiency in constraint-critical regions. The framework is validated on the Three Gorges Reservoir using 60 years (1965–2024) of daily inflow records. Results show that the Lagrangian dual method reduces the total absolute constraint cost by 71.5% and increases generation reward by 4.9% compared with the correction-based baseline. In the baseline evaluation, the FullMask reduces the action-correction violation rate from 21–79% to zero, and the square mapping yields a further 0.54% gain in total energy generation. These results support the proposed SafeRL framework as a model-consistent decision-support approach for long-horizon reservoir operation under the modeled constraints.

recovered_records.title: A physics-informed multi-scale fourier neural operator framework for snow avalanche dynamics simulation
recovered_records.abstract: Avalanches are typical natural disasters in alpine watersheds. Near-real-time early warning and multi-scenario risk assessment require a balance between physical consistency and computational efficiency, yet traditional numerical solvers often suffer from severe computational bottlenecks in high-resolution simulations or large-scale scenario ensemble computations. To address this issue, this study proposes a Physics-Informed Neural Operator (PINO) framework for the efficient prediction of avalanche dynamic processes. The framework uses the Fourier Neural Operator as the backbone network and incorporates residual constraints of governing equations. By introducing architectural enhancements including dimensionless physical loss, a spatial feature extractor, and a channel attention mechanism, the model’s ability to learn complex avalanche evolution processes under varying terrain and physical parameters is significantly improved. Meanwhile, an active-region-prioritized sampling scheme and a progressive training strategy further enhance training efficiency. The model is trained and evaluated solely on 12 heterogeneous multi-scenario datasets generated by the RAMMS software. Results demonstrate that the model achieves relatively stable accuracy under cross-parameter and cross-terrain conditions, and its performance is significantly superior to traditional Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).Its zero-shot super-resolution performance also outperforms the standard FNO. Benchmark tests show that the inference time reaches the near-real-time level of seconds to tens of seconds, providing a feasible and novel paradigm for multi-scenario risk assessment and near-real-time prediction of avalanches and other shallow surface flow dynamic processes in alpine watersheds.

recovered_records.title: Enhancing large-scale streamflow prediction by coupling structural inductive bias with meta-learning
recovered_records.abstract: Deep learning has opened new opportunities for streamflow modeling, enabling the extraction of complex hydrological patterns from large-sample observations. However, large-scale streamflow prediction remains challenging, requiring robust generalization across diverse hydroclimatic conditions and reliable transfer to ungauged regions. To address these challenges, we propose a MAML-EA-LSTM framework that integrates Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) with an entity-aware Long Short-Term Memory (EA-LSTM) architecture. The framework is evaluated using 468 basins from the CAMELS dataset. Results show that the proposed MAML-EA-LSTM achieves a mean Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) of 0.75, outperforming LSTM (0.70), EA-LSTM (0.69), MAML-LSTM (0.71), and the conceptual Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting (SAC-SMA) model (0.57), with improvements observed in most basins. Reductions in both high-flow and low-flow bias further indicate enhanced predictive stability across contrasting hydrological conditions. Dominant attribute identification analysis shows that MAML-EA-LSTM also improves hydrological behavior learning, yielding an overall hit rate of 71.2%, higher than LSTM (43.6%), EA-LSTM (60.7%) and MAML-LSTM (51.5%). Transfer experiments under strictly spatially disjoint conditions further demonstrate stronger out-of-sample transferability in data-scarce basins. The proposed framework achieves an NSE of 0.553 with only one year of target-basin observations for fine-tuning. These findings indicate that the integration of structural inductive bias and meta-learning provides a promising pathway toward more robust and transferable large-sample hydrological modeling.

recovered_records.title: Bridging training–projection gaps in purely data-driven deep learning for runoff under climate change
recovered_records.abstract: Purely data-driven deep learning (DL) models show superior performance in runoff simulation but suffer from a critical training–projection gap, producing physically implausible results under significantly altered climate conditions. This study develops a physics informed Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework that structurally embeds dynamic water balance and evapotranspiration modules to enforce physical consistency. Using the Pearl River Basin (PRB)—China’s second largest by discharge—and three additional subtropical basins as testbeds, we systematically assess the prevalence of this gap and demonstrate the framework’s ability to overcome it. Results show that standard LSTM models, which are purely data-driven, yield anomaly ratios of 61–100% under warming scenarios, often misinterpreting temperature rise as a runoff-generating signal. In contrast, the hybrid framework eliminates anomalous projections while maintaining or improving accuracy relative to process-based and purely data-driven models. The hybrid framework also corrects systematic biases in the PRB under CMIP6 scenarios: standard LSTMs erroneously amplify flood risks (overestimating up to 78 events per decade) and suppress drought signals (underestimating up to 9 events per decade) relative to the physically consistent benchmark provided by the hybrid DL. The model further highlights wet-season intensification in the PRB, with up to 30% increases in annual runoff but sharper seasonal contrasts. These basin- and sub-basin-level insights provide a more reliable scientific basis for climate adaptation strategies. Overall, the proposed framework offers a flexible, physics-encoded architecture that bridges the training–projection gap and advances DL toward more trustworthy hydrological projections under climate change.

recovered_records.title: Climate change impacts on water quality in a groundwater flow-through lake: a hybrid approach combining turbulence modeling and deep learning
recovered_records.abstract: This study examines the effects of climate change on water quality in Gull Lake, a deep inland lake in the Laurentian Great Lakes basin, using an integrated framework that combines the one-dimensional process-based General Ocean Turbulence Model (GOTM) with a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) model. GOTM effectively simulates the lake’s thermal structure, achieving an RMSE of 1.00 °C over the period 2008–2018 by incorporating time-dependent light attenuation coefficients and groundwater interactions. The MLP model predicts key water quality variables, including temperature, dissolved oxygen (DO), and chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), with high accuracy (RMSE: 0.94 °C, 1.47 mg/L, and 0.57 µg/L, respectively) by leveraging thermal structure indicators such as thermocline depth and thickness derived from GOTM. The integrated framework effectively reproduces hypoxic and anoxic conditions, including the number of low-oxygen days. Projected climate forcing under the SSP5–8.5 scenario leads to higher air and lake temperatures, particularly in winter and spring, intensifying thermal stratification and weakening vertical mixing. These changes lead to increased Chl-a concentrations and DO levels, as well as persistent risks of eutrophication, hypoxia, and anoxia. By combining process-based and data-driven approaches, the research demonstrates how climate change, thermal stratification, and water quality dynamics interact in a deep, stratified lake. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for vertical thermal structure when predicting ecological responses to climate change, and provide insights into seasonal patterns and long-term trends in lake water quality dynamics under extreme climate forcing.

recovered_records.title: AI-driven monitoring strategy optimization for nutrient-polluted groundwater in a desert site in Northwest China
recovered_records.abstract: The hydrological cycle drives material transport and energy exchange within Earth’s critical zone while serving as a key conduit for aquifer pollution. Natural attenuation is a cost-effective remediation strategy, yet its implementation is hindered by redundant monitoring indicators and excessive sampling frequency. Current optimization efforts rely on “black models” that lack biogeochemical interpretability and fail to adapt to dynamic attenuation phases. To address these gaps, this study used interpretable Artificial Intelligence (AI) to reveal multi-stage attenuation patterns and the hydrochemical mechanisms controlling pollution at a desert site in Northwest China, enabling mechanism-informed monitoring optimization. Using high-frequency monitoring data, the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified NH4+, Mn, dissolved oxygen (DO), and permanganate index (CODMn) as key determinants of water quality variations. Temporal analysis revealed a novel two-stage natural attenuation mechanism driven by redox heterogeneity. During early rapid attenuation, organic matter (OM) depletion shifted the aquifer to oxidizing conditions, coupling NH4+ nitrification with Mn precipitation. Notably, during the tailing stage, OM released from the vadose zone created localized reducing microenvironments within the broadly oxidizing system, triggering the coupling of Mn oxides dissolution and aerobic denitrification of NO3−, ultimately restoring groundwater quality to background levels. Based on these mechanistic insights, this study proposed a mechanism-driven, endpoint-oriented dynamic monitoring strategy: semimonthly during the rapid stage and quarterly during the tailing stage. These findings offer a perspective on balancing the monitoring costs with regulatory effectiveness in groundwater management.

recovered_records.title: Integrating machine learning with a novel karst hydrological model to enhance extreme streamflow simulation in karst regions
recovered_records.abstract: To improve streamflow simulation accuracy, particularly for extreme flood events in karst regions, this study addresses two key technical challenges: the limited ability of process-based models (PBMs) to represent the complex and highly heterogeneous hydrological processes controlling flood generation in karst systems, and the weak generalization capability of machine learning (ML) models under data-scarce conditions. By incorporating karst medium characteristics and an event-based dry-wet feedback mechanism, we coupled the wet-dry-event Karst SWAT (WDE-KSWAT) model with a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to develop a hybrid framework that integrates physical-process representation and data-driven learning, referred to as the LSTM-WDE-KSWAT model. Using the original SWAT and XGBoost models as benchmarks, we conducted comprehensive evaluations across three representative karst basins (seven hydrological stations) in southwestern China. WDE-KSWAT achieved good performance in all three basins, with mean R2, NSE, and KGE values of 0.76, 0.75, and 0.78 during calibration and 0.73, 0.73, and 0.80 during validation, representing absolute improvements of 0.13–0.20 over the original SWAT model. Overall, the LSTM model outperformed the process-based models and XGBoost, with mean R2, NSE, and KGE values exceeding 0.80 throughout the simulation period. Moreover, the coupled LSTM-WDE-KSWAT model further improved these metrics and demonstrated strong robustness during 28 extreme flood events, with mean values exceeding 0.85, significantly outperforming WDE-KSWAT, LSTM, and XGBoost. SHAP analysis suggests that WDE-KSWAT provides hydrological process variables with clear physical meaning, which contribute more to model predictions than conventional meteorological inputs. These findings highlight the importance of structural enhancements in process-based models and suggest that future hydrological modeling in karst regions can benefit from both advances in data-mining techniques and continued innovation in physical-process representation.

recovered_records.title: Flood inundation monitoring with multi-source satellite imagery based on deep learning and explainable frameworks
recovered_records.abstract: Flood inundation monitoring using satellite data plays a crucial role in emergency response. To harness the advantages of Multispectral (MS) and Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) sensors while mitigating their limitations, an integration of multi-source satellite imagery is crucial. In this study, we introduced U-Net to extract water bodies from scenes captured by Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellites. The performance of the U-Net model was evaluated using both a standard dataset and real-world cases. Different combinations of multi-source satellite imagery were then compared to investigate the variations across images and identify the most effective inputs. Finally, an explainable framework called Grad-CAM was employed to gain insights into the active regions within the deep learning models’ inner layers. The U-Net model achieved strong segmentation performance on Sentinel-1 imagery, with an overall accuracy of 0.95 and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.33. The model produced a 1.41% false-water rate and a 34.62% false-dry rate, both outperforming the baseline. When Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data were jointly used as inputs, overall accuracy increased to 0.97 and IoU increased to 0.33, while the false-positive and false-negative rates decreased to 0.86% and 27.85% respectively, surpassing models trained on either data source alone. Additionally, the incorporation of auxiliary information such as DEM further enhanced the model’s performance. The analysis of the shallow layers revealed their remarkable transparency and emphasized the necessity of introducing deep learning architecture in multi-source satellite imagery applications. This study can help enhance the utilization efficiency of multi-source satellite data and improve the understanding of deep learning models used for monitoring flood inundation.

recovered_records.title: A multi-source precipitation blending method combining hydrological model-guided precipitation adjustment and double transfer learning-based data merging
recovered_records.abstract: Precipitation blending has been established as an effective approach for enhancing quantitative precipitation estimation accuracy. However, conventional precipitation blending methods exhibit two inherent limitations: (1) poor applicability in regions with sparse rain gauge networks; and (2) degraded estimation performance due to insufficient accuracy of input data sources. To address these limitations, this study proposes a multi-source precipitation blending (MSPB) method to integrate three datasets—ground, gridded precipitation, and auxiliary meteorological datasets—characterized by high spatiotemporal resolution and real-time capability. The methodology involves: (1) preprocessing all datasets into standardized input–output structures; (2) implementing an HBV-guided precipitation adjustment (HBV_PA) model to enhance data quality; (3) developing a double transfer learning (DTL) model using the corrected datasets to generate the blended precipitation product; and (4) conducting comprehensive performance evaluation against comparative objects, with demonstration through a case study in the source area of the Yellow River (YRSA). The evaluation metrics include probability of detection (POD), false alarm ratio (FAR), and critical success index (CSI) for event detection, as well as the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE), and root mean square error (RMSE) for quantitative assessment. Results demonstrate that HBV_PA-adjusted precipitation products significantly outperform the three original sources (IMERG-Late, GSMaP-Gauge, and ERA5-Land) across most statistical metrics in both temporal and spatial dimensions. Following the application of DTL to fuse HBV_PA-adjusted multi-source precipitation inputs, the MSPB method exhibits enhanced rainy-event detection performance (POD = 0.87 ± 0.01, FAR = 0.23 ± 0.01, CSI = 0.69 ± 0.01) alongside optimal precipitation quantification capabilities (NSE = 0.46 ± 0.02, KGE = 0.62 ± 0.01, RMSE = 2.28 ± 0.04), and outperforms other multi-source precipitation products and benchmark methods. Benchmark experiments conducted in the Tangnaihai–Lanzhou reach (TLR) further confirm that the proposed DTL model outperforms all benchmark methods by effectively leveraging extra-basin information, offering a superior solution for reliable estimation in data-sparse basins. Contribution analysis further reveals distinctive functional roles of input data sources in merging performance, confirming the substantial contribution of multi-source precipitation data and auxiliary meteorological information to precipitation estimation accuracy. This study establishes the MSPB method as a scalable solution for developing high-precision precipitation products. By integrating physically meaningful adjustments with a powerful transfer learning capability, the framework achieves robust predictive performance while effectively overcoming the critical challenge of in-situ data scarcity in sparsely gauged basins.

recovered_records.title: A hierarchical machine learning framework for reconstructing freezing-period pan evaporation across various climate zones of China
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate estimation of pan evaporation (Epan) during the freezing period is critical for hydrological modeling and water resources management, particularly in cold regions, yet it remains a significant challenge due to operational difficulties, high labor costs, and cumulative observation errors, leading to widespread data gaps. To address this issue, this study proposed a novel hierarchical interpolation strategy that physically bridged the evaporation processes between non-freezing and freezing periods. The framework was structured in three steps: (1) interpolation of non-freezing period Epan using meteorological drivers, (2) introduction and estimation of a freezing-period conversion coefficient (Tf) to quantify the suppression effect of freezing conditions, and (3) reconstruction of freezing-period Epan by integrating the outputs of the first two steps. Four models—multivariate polynomial regression, multivariate adaptive regression splines (MARS), support vector regression (SVR), and extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost)—were evaluated at 705 stations across five climate zones of China. Results demonstrated that XGBoost and SVR performed best for non-freezing period Epan interpolation (mean R2 = 0.90, RMSE = 0.99 mm d−1) and the final freezing-period Epan reconstruction (mean R2 = 0.84, RMSE = 0.40 mm d−1). MARS excelled in Tf estimation (mean R2 = 0.72, RMSE = 0.12 mm d−1), capturing complex freezing mechanisms. For applications, XGBoost is recommended for its accuracy and efficiency, while MARS offers advantages in ungauged areas through explicit equations. This work provides a robust, physics-based framework for generating continuous freezing-period Epan data, supporting improved hydrological modeling and climate adaptation in cold regions.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed deep learning for hillslope subsurface flow prediction: integrating soil moisture deficit constraints
recovered_records.abstract: Accurate simulation of hillslope subsurface stormflow (SSF) is critical for understanding runoff generation in headwater catchments, regulating flood responses, and constraining biogeochemical fluxes. However, SSF dynamics are inherently intermittent and strongly threshold-controlled, emerging only when antecedent soil moisture and rainfall jointly exceed critical storage conditions. While deep learning can handle these complex processes, purely data-driven models often lack physical consistency, resulting in inaccurate predictions, especially in data-scarce or changing environments. In this study, we develop a physics-informed deep learning framework to better represent moisture-controlled activation processes in hillslope rainfall–runoff dynamics. Using a unique, high-frequency decadal dataset (2015–2025) from the Hemuqiao hydrological experimental station, we systematically evaluate multiple deep learning architectures and identify the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network as the most reliable backbone for representing intermittent SSF, outperforming both Transformer-based and convolutional models. We also found that the antecedent soil moisture index (ASI) is the key variable controlling flow initiation. We therefore embed ASI-based physical constraints through two complementary strategies: a hard constraint, implemented as a mechanistic input transformation that gates rainfall based on soil moisture deficits, and a soft constraint, introduced through physics-informed loss regularization. The results reveal a pronounced state dependence in their effectiveness. Hard constraints are particularly beneficial under dry conditions, where strict deficit thresholds suppress false-positive flow predictions; whereas soft constraints perform better in wet states by preserving the model’s flexibility to capture nonlinear high-flow responses. Event-based analyses further demonstrate that compared to large rainfall events, the minor rainfall events play a foundational role in PIDL modeling due to their importance in identifying the threshold of subsurface stormflow generation. Together, these findings highlight that embedding physical constraints into deep learning models substantially improves both predictive skill and hydrological consistency.

recovered_records.title: Deep learning for decoding climate–urbanization synergies: flood susceptibility forecasting under SSP-RCP scenarios in Beijing, China
recovered_records.abstract: Climate change and urbanization amplify urban pluvial flooding susceptibility, threatening sustainable development. Traditional methods for assessing flood susceptibility, such as numerical simulations and single machine learning models, exhibit limitations when confronted with spatial heterogeneity, dynamic environmental factors, and high-dimensional data. These constraints hinder the advancement of flood prediction accuracy. We propose an interpretable hybrid deep learning framework to map and project urban flood susceptibility under climate-urbanization synergies, using megacity Beijing as a testbed. Spatial heterogeneity is addressed through Optimal Parameter Geodetector and Boruta algorithms to identify key drivers. Our Hybrid SNN-KAN-Attention model integrates: (1) an Spiking Neural Networks (SNN)-based spike encoder to enhance the nonlinear representation of static conditioning factors, (2) Knowledge Adaptive Networks (KAN) to decode nonlinear driver relationships, and (3) Attention mechanisms capturing spatial heterogeneity. The SHAP interpretation model, alongside Partial Dependence Plots (PDP), is integrated to examine the nonlinear driving mechanisms of the key factors and simulate the spatial and temporal evolution of flood susceptibility for the period 2020–2100 based on the coupled SSP-RCP scenarios. Results demonstrate the hybrid model’s superiority over traditional methods, achieving 0.88 accuracy (10%–20% improvement), 0.93 AUC, with ablation studies confirming the criticality of attention and KAN modules. The primary drivers of flood susceptibility identified include distance to roads, soil type, and road network density. Projections reveal Beijing’s flood susceptibility will intensify with climate-urbanization synergies, exhibiting 23%–41% high- susceptibility area expansion by 2100, particularly under SSP5-8.5. Overall, the proposed framework improves susceptibility prediction accuracy and interpretability, providing practical evidence to support climate-adaptive urban planning and, when combined with exposure/vulnerability information, subsequent flood risk management.

recovered_records.title: Damming effects on bankfull channel geometry in the Lower Yellow River: adjustment patterns and a physics-informed machine learning framework
recovered_records.abstract: Damming typically alters natural flow-sediment dynamics, triggering significant changes in riverbed morphology. Understanding and predicting these morphological responses is critical for sustainable river management. Vertical incision over large longitudinal extents caused by dams has received widespread attention, but the role of lateral width in bed morphology adjustment in unstable dammed channel systems (e.g., braided and transitional rivers) has received comparatively less attention. Theoretically, bankfull channel geometry adjustments can be classified into eight distinct patterns based on variations in width and bed elevation. Using 22 years of bathymetric data (2000–2021) collected since the full operation of the Xiaolangdi Dam commenced, this study investigates these adjustment patterns at multiscale in the braided and transitional reaches of the Lower Yellow River. We identify key controlling factors, including flow-sediment regimes, antecedent cross-sectional geometry, bed grain size, and channel slope. A hybrid physics-informed machine learning model combining Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Support Vector Regression (SVR) was proposed to predict these adjustment patterns. At the cross-sectional scale, six dominant adjustment patterns emerged: (Ⅰ) aggrading with widening, (II) aggrading with narrowing, (III) degrading with narrowing, (Ⅳ) degrading with widening, (Ⅵ) exclusive aggrading, and (VIII) exclusive degrading. At the reach scale, only three patterns were observed: I, III, and IV. Pattern IV (degrading with widening) was the most prevalent at both scales. Morphological adjustments through degrading with widening collectively increased bankfull area. In the braided reach, lateral widening contributed more than vertical degradation to bankfull area expansion in 27% of cross-sections, compared to 16% in the transitional reach. The reach-scale analysis reveals that in the braided reach, widening and incision accounted for 40% and 60% of the bankfull area increase, respectively, whereas in the transitional reach, the proportions were 22% and 78%. Channel widening induced by damming plays a non-negligible role in shaping channel morphology, particularly in braided reach. The braided reach experiences more severe lateral erosion due to its stronger stream power, weaker bank resistance, and lower river engineering confinement. The proposed PSO-SVR model demonstrated strong predictive performance, achieving approximately 80% accuracy at the cross-sectional scale and approximately 90% at the reach scale. This study offers a representative case of large alluvial river responses to dam-induced perturbations across varying channel patterns and provides a predictive framework for managing regulated fluvial systems.

recovered_records.title: A DeepONet surrogate for accelerating distributed hydrological model simulations
recovered_records.abstract: Distributed hydrological models are the mainstream paradigm for watershed hydrological simulation, integrating heterogeneous factors through spatial discretization and demonstrating significant advantages in revealing the spatial differentiation patterns of hydrological processes. However, the high-dimensional parameter space leads to high computational costs and low robustness in parameter calibration in traditional distributed hydrological models. Taking Weihe River Basin and Water Allocation and Cycle Model (WACM), a traditional distributed hydrological model, as the study area and base model, this study proposed a surrogate Deep Neural Operator (DeepONet) model to enhance the calibration efficiency. The surrogate DeepONet uses a branch network to project the high-dimensional model parameters into a compact latent space and a trunk network to encode the spatiotemporal coordinates of runoff outputs, jointly learning a nonlinear mapping from parameters to runoff that replaces direct calibration in the original parameter space and thus greatly reduces both the effective parameter dimensionality and the computational cost of calibration. The results show that the median Kling–Gupta Efficiency (KGE) coefficient across all gauging stations exceeds 0.85, whereas the parameter calibration time is reduced to less than 10% of that required by traditional genetic algorithms. In addition, the surrogate model achieved high accuracy in runoff prediction, with KGE values above 0.80 at these ungauged stations. This study demonstrates that the deep integration of physical mechanisms and data-driven approaches can effectively enhance the trade-off in the efficiency-accuracy dilemma in hydrological simulations and presents a sound solution for high-dimensional parameter calibration in distributed hydrological models.

recovered_records.title: A hybrid method coupling physical process-driven model with generative deep learning for probabilistic flood forecasting

However, singular models often face challenges to maintain high capability in physical interpretability, forecast accuracy, and uncertainty quantification. This study proposed a hybrid model that couples a process-driven model with generative deep learning method. First, a probabilistic forecasting framework that couples the process-driven model with a data-driven model was developed. The forecast error series was obtained via rolling forecasts based on XAJ model. Subsequently, a Conditional Diffusion Model (CDM) was developed to learn the stochastic characteristics and temporal dependencies of multiple variables implicitly and then generate high-quality ensembles of forecast errors. Finally, the probabilistic forecast results were obtained by combining deterministic forecast results with generated error ensembles. The effectiveness of the proposed method was evaluated using historical flood events in the Longhekou Reservoir of the Chaohu Lake Basin, China. Compared with the benchmark XAJ-VC, the average NSE of XAJ-CDM was above 0.9, and the average RMSE and MAE decreased by 16.05%-72.48% within the 1–7 h lead time. Meanwhile, the average CR has increased by 19.45%, while the average RB and CRPS decreased by 54.88% and 63.98% respectively. In the vast majority of flood events, XAJ-CDM has better accuracy and reliability compared to the benchmark model. This study provides a feasible framework for coupling generative deep learning method with process-driven models. The findings highlight the potential of novel data-driven models and hybrid modeling methods in enhancing the accuracy and reliability of flood forecasts.

recovered_records.title: Physics-informed machine learning with embedded sediment rating curve constraints for high-fidelity multi-lead-time forecast of suspended sediment concentration
recovered_records.abstract: Suspended sediment concentration (SSC) critically influences fluvial morphodynamics, sediment transport, and ecological health. Its forecast is hindered by nonlinear, nonstationary dynamics driven by hydrologic variability and multiscale interactions. Conventional models often fail to capture these complexities, necessitating adaptive, physics-informed approaches. This study developed a physics-informed machine learning framework that embeds empirical sediment rating curves as differentiable regularization terms within MLP-SGD and XGBoost loss functions. Two formulations were tested: the single-regime equation of Fernández et al. (2018) and a novel, threshold-based piecewise curve. Evaluated on daily discharge (Q) and SSC data (1982–2022) from Chester (CH) and Thebes (TH) stations on the lower Upper Mississippi River, the advanced Physics-informed eXtreme Gradient Boosting Tree model with six inputs (APhyXGBoost-6), integrating current Q and three-day antecedent SSC and Q, achieved R2 = 0.981 (CH) and 0.986 (TH), surpassing conventional XGBoost by 15.5–16.1% in R2 and reducing scatter index by over 66%. It accurately replicated extreme SSC events and the heavy-tailed distribution, maintaining skill up to 14-day lead times. Under high-flow conditions, where empirical rating curves failed (NSE < − 16), APhyXGBoost-6 retained high fidelity (R2 > 0.95). Performance peaked when real-time discharge was combined with antecedent sediment memory, reflecting physical coupling of hydraulic forcing and sediment availability. Critically, it reproduced observed clockwise hysteresis loops during major floods (2013–2019), with predicted Hysteresis Index values matching observations within a mean absolute error of 0.02. This work establishes a generalizable framework for embedding regime-aware knowledge into data-driven models, advancing operational SSC forecasting in complex river systems.
